notes.h: Key concepts: unionism, militarism and democracy
notes.b: Three terms run through the story of Ulster resistance to Home Rule (a separate parliament in Dublin for Irish affairs, with Ireland still under the Crown). Each has a specific meaning in this topic.
points: Unionism was the movement to keep Ireland in the United Kingdom and to oppose Home Rule. Its supporters were called unionists.

Militarism, as used here, means using armed, drilled volunteer forces as a political tool, so that the threat of force stands behind a political demand. The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), formed in 1913, is the main example.

Democracy means rule by the elected majority. Nationalists said unionist threats of force defied democracy, because they were meant to overrule a Home Rule Bill passed by the elected House of Commons.
Unionists answered that Ulster must consent to its own government, so a Dublin parliament could not rightly be imposed on it against its will.
notes.tip: In documents-based questions, explain that the unionist demand was Ulster’s consent, and look at the purpose and bias of each source, whether unionist or nationalist.

notes.b: Unionism was a coalition of Protestants of all classes in Ulster with landlords and business people elsewhere in Ireland, united by opposition to a Dublin parliament. It was never simply ‘all Protestants’.
points: Ulster had a slight Protestant majority (about 56 per cent in 1911), concentrated in the east. Antrim, Down, Armagh and Londonderry had Protestant majorities, while Tyrone and Fermanagh had narrow Catholic majorities, which is why these two counties later became hard to settle.

Protestants of every class were unionist: landlords and gentry, industrialists, shopkeepers, Presbyterian tenant farmers and Protestant workers in Belfast. Shared fear of Home Rule, not shared wealth, held them together.

Southern unionists were a small minority (Protestants were about a tenth of the population outside Ulster), made up of landlords, professionals, businessmen and Church of Ireland clergy, strongest in Dublin and parts of Munster and Leinster.
Gladstone, the Liberal leader, announced his conversion to Home Rule in December 1885, and the First Home Rule Bill was defeated in the Commons in June 1886.
Most Ulster Presbyterians had supported the Liberals before 1886, so Gladstone’s conversion pushed many of them into the unionist camp.

Many Protestants had already been alarmed by Gladstone’s disestablishment of the Church of Ireland (the Irish Church Act of 1869, which ended its status as the state church) and by the Land Acts of 1870 and 1881, and they saw Home Rule as the next step.
Colonel Edward Saunderson led the Irish Unionist MPs at Westminster from 1886 until his death in 1906. Walter Long followed him, and Carson took over in February 1910.
notes.tip: Use ‘unionist’ for the political movement and remember the southern minority: not every Protestant was a unionist. Know the leaders in order: Saunderson (to 1906), Long (1906–10), Carson (from 1910).

notes.h: Why unionists opposed Home Rule: religion and economy
notes.b: Unionists opposed Home Rule for three linked reasons: religion, economics, and identity and empire. Two of them were fears about everyday life, namely what a Catholic majority might do and what a Dublin parliament might do to Belfast’s trade.
points: Religion: Protestants feared that a parliament elected by a Catholic majority would be under Catholic Church influence. The slogan was that Home Rule is Rome Rule.
The Ne Temere decree (effective 1908) required the children of mixed marriages to be brought up Catholic, and unionists cited it as later support for the fear of Catholic Church influence.

Economy: Belfast’s linen, shipbuilding (Harland and Wolff), engineering and rope-making depended on British and imperial markets and raw materials, so unionists feared tariffs and higher taxes under a Dublin parliament.

Ulster’s industrial north-east had a different economy from the agricultural south and west, so unionists argued that an Irish parliament would favour agricultural interests at the expense of industry.
notes.tip: Exam answers name the three reasons (religion, economy, identity and empire) and then link each to the organisation unionists built, with dated examples.

notes.h: Why unionists opposed Home Rule: identity, minority fears and the Union
notes.b: The third reason was about who unionists believed they were, and it was joined by fears of life as a minority and by an argument that went beyond Ulster.
points: Identity and empire: Ulster Protestants saw themselves as British, were proud of the empire, and believed that Home Rule was the first step towards separation from Britain.

Protestants also feared for their position as a minority in a self-governing Ireland, and many believed nationalists would dispossess them, as they thought the Land War (the campaign against landlords) had shown.

Many Ulster unionists believed that the Land Acts and the Irish Party’s links with Fenians (members of the revolutionary movement for an Irish republic) showed that nationalists would not respect property.

Joseph Chamberlain and Lord Hartington led the Liberal Unionists, who voted against the 1886 Bill. They argued that Home Rule would threaten the integrity of the United Kingdom, not only the Ulster minority.

notes.b: From 1885 unionists built organisations to match the nationalist National League. Each new body answered a particular threat, which is why the order of dates matters.
points: The Orange Order, founded in 1795 after the Battle of the Diamond in County Armagh, revived in the 1880s and gave Ulster unionism a mass base of lodges across the province.
The Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union was founded in Dublin in 1885 by southern unionists. The Ulster Loyalist Anti-Repeal Union followed in 1886.

In February 1886 the Conservative Lord Randolph Churchill urged unionists to “play the Orange card”, meaning to use Ulster Protestant feeling against Home Rule, and said “Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right”.
Belfast riots in summer 1886, in which several were killed, sharpened sectarian division. There is more on this in the notes on the 1885–86 elections.
The Irish Unionist Alliance was formed in 1891 to unite the Irish unionist bodies.
The Ulster Convention met in the Botanic Gardens, Belfast, on 17 June 1892, with about 12,000 delegates. It protested against the coming Second Home Rule Bill, and a Dublin convention followed.
The Second Home Rule Bill (1893) passed the Commons but was defeated in the Lords in September 1893, so unionist resistance had not yet been put to the test.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Ulster Convention (1892) with Ulster Day (1912), or the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union (southern, 1885), the Irish Unionist Alliance (1891) and the Ulster Unionist Council (1905).

notes.b: By the early 1900s unionists needed a permanent central body for Ulster, and later they drew women into the movement as well.
points: Lord Dunraven’s Irish Reform Association (1904) proposed limited devolution (giving Ireland some self-government short of Home Rule), which alarmed Ulster unionists.
This 1904–05 devolution scare convinced Ulster unionists that they needed their own permanent body, so the Ulster Unionist Council was founded in March 1905 (first meeting 3 March).
The Council brought together Orange lodges, constituency associations and unionist MPs, so it joined the mass base, the local organisers and the parliamentary leaders in one body.
The Ulster Women’s Unionist Council, formed in January 1911 under its president Lady Londonderry, mobilised tens of thousands of women for the unionist cause.
notes.tip: Be ready to give the reason for the Ulster Unionist Council (the devolution scare) and who it united, since short-answer questions ask for both.

notes.b: Carson, a Dublin-born barrister, led the unionist campaign against the Third Home Rule Bill and made the threat of armed resistance credible.
points: Edward Carson (born in Dublin on 9 February 1854, died 1935) was educated at Trinity College and became a leading barrister. In 1895 he cross-examined Oscar Wilde as counsel for the Marquess of Queensberry, after which Wilde lost his libel case and was prosecuted.

He was Solicitor General for Ireland and MP for Dublin University from 1892 (to 1918), and Solicitor General for England in 1900–06 (knighted 1900). In February 1910 he succeeded Walter Long as leader of the Irish Unionist parliamentary party, and he was the chief unionist campaigner from 1911 to 1914.
He was a leading participant: he spoke at the Craigavon rally, led the Ulster Day campaign on 28 September 1912 and signed the Covenant first at Belfast City Hall.
He was chairman of the Provisional Government plan of 1913, rejected Asquith’s county option in 1914 and took part in the Buckingham Palace Conference.

He made the threat of resistance credible, but James Craig’s organisation and Conservative backing gave it force. His Dublin background made him an unlikely leader of Ulster, but he spoke for all Irish unionists.
Contemporary unionists revered him as the defender of the Union. Nationalists and many Liberals thought him a man ready to defy Parliament, and Redmond denounced the threat of force.
Historians differ: some say he never intended to fight and bluffed to protect the Union; others that his threat made partition inevitable and that he left southern unionists exposed.
He resigned the Ulster Unionist leadership in February 1921 (Craig succeeded him) and became a law lord (Lord of Appeal) that year, the year Northern Ireland came into being.
notes.tip: A profile needs his Dublin birth and barrister background, his 1910 leadership, the 1912 Covenant and the 1913 Provisional Government plan; a longer answer adds a judgement on success and failure, with contemporary and historians’ views. Do not call him an Ulsterman, and do not confuse Carson (leader) with Craig (organiser).

notes.h: The Third Home Rule crisis (1911–1912): Craig, the Bill and Blenheim
notes.b: After the Parliament Act of 1911 removed the Lords’ power to block Home Rule, unionists organised a campaign of mass resistance with Conservative backing.
points: The Parliament Act (royal assent, August 1911) meant that the Lords could delay a Bill for two years but not block it, so Home Rule could now become law within about two years.

James Craig (born 1871), a wealthy Belfast whiskey-fortune businessman and MP for East Down from 1906, became Carson’s chief organiser and planned the campaign. He later became the first Prime Minister of Northern Ireland (1921).
A huge unionist demonstration was held at Craigavon, outside Belfast, in September 1911, with Carson as speaker. Tens of thousands attended.

The Third Home Rule Bill was introduced by Asquith on 11 April 1912. An amendment to exclude Antrim, Down, Armagh and Londonderry, moved by the Liberal Thomas Agar-Robartes, was defeated in June 1912.

Andrew Bonar Law, Conservative leader since November 1911, spoke at Blenheim Palace on 27 July 1912: “I can imagine no length of resistance to which Ulster can go in which I should not be prepared to support them.” This pledged his party to back Ulster.
notes.tip: Short answers ask who, what and when: Craigavon (September 1911), Blenheim (27 July 1912) and Craig as organiser. Learn each as a one-line fact.

notes.h: Ulster Day and the Bill’s passage, 1912–1914
notes.b: The unionist campaign reached its peak with the Covenant, while the Third Home Rule Bill moved slowly through Parliament.
points: On Ulster Day, 28 September 1912, about 237,000 men signed the Solemn League and Covenant, and Carson signed first, at Belfast City Hall. Signatories pledged to “use all means which may be found necessary to defeat the present conspiracy to set up a Home Rule Parliament in Ireland”.
About 234,000 women signed a separate declaration, so about 471,000 signed in all, which showed how wide the support was.
The Twelfth of July Orange demonstrations and Presbyterian and Church of Ireland ministers gave the campaign a religious character, with many ministers joining Covenant services.
The Commons passed the Third Home Rule Bill in January 1913 and the Lords rejected it (30 January 1913). The same happened in July 1913.
The Commons passed the Bill a third time in May 1914, so under the Parliament Act it could go for royal assent without the Lords’ consent.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Covenant of Ulster Day (1912) with the Ulster Convention (1892).

notes.h: The Ulster Volunteer Force and the Provisional Government (1913)
notes.b: In 1913 unionist leaders organised an armed force and prepared to take over the government of Ulster. This is militarism in practice, with drilled volunteers used to back a political demand.
points: The Ulster Volunteer Force was formed in January 1913 from earlier local drilling clubs. Its commander was Lieutenant-General Sir George Richardson, a retired Indian Army officer.
By 1914 the UVF had about 90,000 or more members, organised in battalions, with many drilling openly and wearing uniform.
On 24 September 1913 the Ulster Unionist Council announced a Provisional Government of Ulster, with Carson as chairman, to take office if Home Rule became law.
Unionists said that they were loyal to the king but not to a Dublin parliament they believed to be illegitimate.

The government did not prosecute. Redmond warned that this failure to act encouraged separatist counter-organisation, and the nationalist Irish Volunteers were founded on 25 November 1913 at the Rotunda Rink, Dublin.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the UVF (unionist, January 1913) with the Irish Volunteers (nationalist, November 1913), and do not claim the UVF fought in 1914: it drilled and armed but did not fight.

notes.h: 1914 (1): the county option and the Curragh incident
notes.b: In March 1914 the government tried a compromise and then discovered that it could not be sure of the army.
points: On 9 March 1914 Asquith proposed that any Ulster county could vote itself out of Home Rule for six years. Carson rejected this as “a sentence of death with a stay of execution for six years”.

On 20 March 1914, in the Curragh incident (County Kildare), Brigadier-General Hubert Gough and most of his cavalry officers (57 of about 70) said they would accept dismissal rather than act against Ulster.
It was not a mutiny, because no order had been refused in action. Critics used the word, but the officers only said they would accept dismissal.

The War Minister, John Seely, and the army chief, Sir John French, resigned at the end of March. The incident showed that the government could not be sure the army would enforce Home Rule in Ulster, which narrowed its options.
notes.tip: Call it the Curragh incident, not the Curragh mutiny. Do not confuse Asquith’s March 1914 county option with the Buckingham Palace Conference in July.

notes.b: While the politicians argued, the UVF armed itself, and the authorities did nothing to stop it.
points: On the night of 24–25 April 1914 the UVF landed about 25,000 rifles and a few million rounds of ammunition, bought in Germany and organised by Major Fred Crawford.
The guns were landed mainly at Larne, and also at Bangor and Donaghadee. The ship was the Clyde Valley.
The weapons were distributed across Ulster by car overnight. Police and army did not stop it, and the government did not prosecute, so unionists had shown that they could arm without penalty.
The Larne landing prompted nationalists to organise their own gun-running at Howth (26 July 1914) and Kilcoole (1–2 August 1914).
notes.tip: Short answers ask for the Larne date and organiser. Attribute Larne to the UVF, and Howth and Kilcoole to nationalists, never to unionists.

notes.h: 1914 (3): the failure of exclusion and the suspended Act
notes.b: With both sides armed, the last attempt to agree on exclusion (leaving part of Ulster outside Home Rule) was a conference called by the king.
points: The Buckingham Palace Conference (21–24 July 1914) was called by George V and chaired by the Speaker, James Lowther. Asquith, Lloyd George, Redmond, Dillon, Carson, Craig, Lansdowne and Bonar Law attended.
It failed over the extent of exclusion, above all Tyrone and Fermanagh, which had mixed populations and narrow Catholic majorities, so neither side could claim them.

By mid-1914 the Amending Bill proposed six-year exclusion of counties by option. Carson insisted on permanent exclusion of Ulster (or six counties), because temporary exclusion was not enough for him.
Nationalists resisted partition and accepted at most temporary exclusion, so the gap was never closed before the war.
The Home Rule Act and the Suspensory Act received royal assent on 18 September 1914, and Home Rule was suspended for the duration of the war, leaving Ulster’s status unsettled.
notes.tip: Do not claim that Home Rule was never passed: it became law on 18 September 1914 and was suspended. Know who attended the conference and why it failed.

notes.b: Judgements on unionism compare its success in blocking Home Rule before 1914 with its failure to hold the whole of Ireland in the Union.
points: Achievement: unionists defeated two Home Rule Bills (the First in 1886 and the Second in 1893), built effective organisation and mobilised mass support.
Achievement: by 1914 they had forced the government to accept the principle of exclusion for Ulster, and Home Rule was suspended in 1914.
Achievement: the UVF, the Covenant and Conservative support showed that Ulster could not be coerced, and made Carson and Craig decisive in later negotiations.

Limit: unionists could not stop the Third Home Rule Bill becoming law, and southern unionists were left unprotected because exclusion concerned only Ulster. Unionism itself was divided between Ulster and the south.
Limit: the Conservative alliance meant unionism was exposed when the Conservatives themselves compromised, as they did in 1920–21.
Contemporary nationalists thought unionist arms threatened democracy and parliament, while unionists thought them a legitimate defence of rights.
A.T.Q. Stewart (The Ulster Crisis, 1967) shows how close Britain came to civil war in 1914, and Alvin Jackson stresses unionist resilience and the divisions between Ulster and southern unionists.
notes.tip: For effectiveness questions, pair achievements (two Bills defeated, exclusion conceded in principle, Home Rule suspended) with limits (the Bill became law, southern unionists unprotected, reliance on the Conservatives), and state a balanced verdict. Be ready to list four or five achievements, each with a fact. In a Carson and Redmond comparison, set Carson’s mobilisation of resistance against Redmond’s Act on the statute book, and compare methods (threat of force against constitutional) and results (partition against delay).

keyTerms.definition: The movement to keep Ireland in the United Kingdom under the Westminster parliament and to oppose Home Rule.
The use of armed volunteer forces as a political tool, as the Ulster Volunteer Force did from 1913.
Rule by the elected majority; nationalists said unionist threats of force defied it, and unionists said Ulster was entitled to its own consent.
The unionist slogan that a Dublin parliament would be dominated by the Catholic Church.
The Protestant society founded in 1795 whose lodges gave Ulster unionism a mass base.
The unionist organisation founded in 1885 by southern unionists to oppose Home Rule.
The central body of Ulster unionism, founded in March 1905.
The pledge to resist Home Rule signed by about 237,000 men on 28 September 1912.
The armed unionist force formed in January 1913 to resist Home Rule.
The March 1914 crisis in which army officers at the Curragh offered to resign rather than act against Ulster.
